  "text": "The council installed the public telephone three days after my mother’s funeral.

It stood outside my flat, bright yellow, with no coin slot and only one button.

At midnight, it rang.

I let it ring for seven nights.

On the eighth, a neighbour leaned out of her window and shouted, “Some of us have people we’re trying to forget.”

I went downstairs.

The receiver was warm.

“Hello, darling,” Mum said. “Have you eaten?”

I sat on the pavement until dawn, telling her everything except that she was dead.

After that, I answered every night.

She asked ordinary questions. Was work all right? Had I fixed the bathroom lock? Did I still keep the spare key beneath the blue pot?

Sometimes I heard cutlery behind her. Sometimes a chair scraping closer.

“Have you got company?” I asked.

“Just the man who lets me call.”

Last night, her voice sounded faint.

“He says we’ve nearly used up our time.”

“How do we get more?”

A pause. Then paper rustling.

“He needs you to press the button.”

I looked at the telephone’s single black button.

“What does it do?”

Mum began to cry.

Behind her, a man whispered something.

“It opens the door,” she said.

I put down the receiver.

The telephone rang again before I reached my building.

Then my mobile rang.

Then every flat above me lit up, one window after another.

Through my open bathroom window, I heard the lock slide shut.

My mother called down softly.

“Darling, where’s the blue pot?”"
